strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real challenges in fine-grained MoE training with clear quantitative evidence (Equation 4, Figure 3, Table 1)
Technically sound memory-efficient backward pass algorithm achieving minimum activation memory (O(2Td + 4TKn)) matching dense models, with clever dS computation avoiding Y and dY caching
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation with extensive kernel-level profiling, multiple strong baselines, thorough ablation studies (Section E), and fair comparisons
Meaningful practical speedups (45% memory reduction, 1.86x forward/backward throughput on H100) with end-to-end validation (213B tokens/day on 64 H100s)
Novel contributions in gathering fusion for backward K-dimension GEMM and application of Ping-Pong scheduling to address MoE's heavy epilogues
Reproducibility and accessibility through open-source implementation in CuTe-DSL, detailed algorithms, extensive configuration tables, and ablation studies
Token rounding routing provides simple yet effective solution to tile quantization with bounded deviation guarantee and empirical quality preservation (16% speedup in sparse settings)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily co-designs existing techniques (gather fusion, Ping-Pong scheduling, dS optimization) rather than introducing fundamental innovations; similar ideas acknowledged in prior work (ScatterMoE, MoMoE, Flash Attention 3, Megatron)

GPU-specific optimizations with limited portability: heavily tailored to Hopper/Blackwell architectures (TMA, WGMMA, Tensor Memory); Blackwell gather fusion requires workarounds (relay mechanism); unclear generalization to other vendors or older architectures
Incremental improvements over existing work: ~40% speedup over ScatterMoE is substantial but not transformative; some configurations show modest improvements (e.g., 7B backward: 8.3% over ScatterMoE)

Token rounding evaluation limited to small models (0.5B/1.4B for full train-eval); inference uses standard TC routing (not TR), limiting practical benefit to training phase; performance degrades when T̄_e/M_tile = 1; method is microbatch-level with unclear interaction with dynamic shapes

Experimental scope: end-to-end training mostly on 7B models; largest model (DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, 685B) only kernel-level benchmarking; limited Blackwell results; would benefit from larger-scale end-to-end training validation

Dense presentation with scattered technical details obscuring main insights; 17-page main paper plus extensive appendix; multiple design choices (Figure 9 strategies, rounding subroutines) lack unified justification
Activation memory claim is slightly weakened: temporary Y variable still materialized (footnote 8), though transient allocation strategy mitigates this
Missing comparisons with recent methods like TMA-adaptive FP8 Grouped GEMM; limited discussion of distributed training with expert parallelism or alternative approaches

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear analysis of how MoE granularity/sparsity impacts hardware efficiency (arithmetic intensity analysis in Section 2.2)
Thorough experimental evaluation across multiple scales (1.4B-120B models) with detailed kernel-level profiling and comprehensive ablations
Multiple complementary optimizations (algorithmic, architectural, and routing) addressing different bottlenecks in fine-grained sparse MoE training
Strong kernel-level improvements demonstrated (1.86x TFLOPS on forward pass, 83-115% improvement over baselines on backward)
Comprehensive appendices with implementation details, design justifications, and ablation studies supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: memory optimization is straightforward recomputation tradeoff, IO overlapping reuses existing FlashAttention-3 techniques, and token rounding is a simple heuristic that rounds frequencies to tile multiples
Hardware-specificity severely limits generalizability—entire system optimized for NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell only; no applicability to other accelerators (TPUs, AMD, etc.)

Modest end-to-end impact despite significant kernel improvements: 213B tokens/day on 64 H100s vs 225B on 96 H100s (50% GPU efficiency gain) is meaningful but not transformative for top-tier conference bar

Token rounding evaluation limited to small models (≤1.4B), only 11 downstream tasks, unclear train-test gap when using token rounding at train time but token-choice at inference; T̄_e/M_tile ≥ 2 constraint lacks theoretical justification

Fairness concerns in comparisons: custom-optimized DeepGEMM implementations rather than original library, MegaBlocks cannot support certain configs, and Triton-based baselines conflate language limitations with algorithmic merit
Dense presentation (34 pages total) with non-standard kernel designs (Algorithm 3's simultaneous dH/dS/A' computation) obscuring core insights; key design motivations explained after the fact

Missing analysis of scalability to very large models (100B+), interaction with distributed training/expert parallelism (deferred to future work), and absolute activation memory benefits in practical training setups
Claims of 'minimum activation memory' and 'SOTA throughput' are qualified by restrictive assumptions (no GEMM recomputation, specific hardware) that are not always stated upfront

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real bottleneck in modern fine-grained, sparse MoE training with clear evidence (Tables 1, 3; Figure 3)

Technically sound and comprehensive: elegant activation memory optimization via reformulated gradient computation; systematic IO-overlapping strategy with extensive ablations validating each component

Impressive experimental validation: kernel-level profiling (Figure 6), multiple model scales (1.4B-120B), end-to-end training results, 11 downstream tasks, robust quality preservation in token rounding
Strong reproducibility: open-sourced code, detailed algorithms, comprehensive configurations enabling reproduction; extensive ablation studies on design choices, tile sizes, microbatch effects
Significant practical impact: 45% activation memory reduction, 1.86x single-layer throughput improvement addressing real LLM scaling challenges with immediate applicability
Clear presentation: logical progression from motivation to algorithm to kernels to routing; informative figures with detailed runtime breakdowns; well-organized appendices
weaknesses: Hardware specificity limits generalizability: optimizations tailored to NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell GPUs with architecture-specific features (ping-pong scheduling, TMA, 2-CTA clusters); reduced applicability to AMD GPUs, TPUs, or other accelerators

Token rounding contribution is incremental: core idea of rounding token counts to tile multiples is straightforward with limited theoretical analysis; quality evaluation restricted to 0.5B-1.4B models; Table 7 shows noticeable degradation at T̄ₑ/M_tile=1 without deep exploration

Gap between per-layer and end-to-end gains: 1.86x per-layer speedup but only ~1.35x efficiency gain per GPU in end-to-end training (213B vs 225B tokens/day); substantial gap warrants deeper analysis of communication overhead and distributed training bottlenecks largely absent from paper

Activation memory analysis limitations: 45% reduction relies on specific gradient computation formulation (dS = ⟨dA'ₑ,ₜ, Aₑ,ₜ⟩) and expert weighting placement; claim of 'minimum activation memory' is domain-specific; temporary Y materialization justification (footnote 9) is hand-wavy

Limited baseline comparisons: missing recent techniques like TMA-adaptive FP8; DeepGEMM comparison uses author-optimized versions ('DeepGEMM++') complicating fair assessment; no exploration of combinations with low-precision training or quantization

Model quality evaluation not comprehensive: downstream tasks limited to 11 small-scale benchmarks without MMLU; token rounding quality only validated at ≤1.4B scale; unclear if benefits extend to 30B+ models where quality sensitivity may differ

Reproducibility constraints: requires H100/Blackwell GPUs for exact reproduction; CuTe DSL is specialized with immature ecosystem; distributed training details (FSDP-2, lm-engine) sparse in main paper

Limited trade-off discussion: gather fusion adds scheduling complexity (2-CTA relay mechanism) without development cost analysis; no code complexity comparisons; insufficient guidance on when practitioners should adopt these techniques or handling edge cases

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real challenges in modern fine-grained and sparse MoE training
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple baselines, GPU generations, and model scales with detailed kernel-level profiling
Concrete and significant practical improvements: 45% memory reduction, 1.86x throughput speedup, demonstrated large-scale training
Solid engineering with multiple well-integrated optimization techniques (gather fusion, epilogue fusion, async IO overlapping)
Thorough ablation studies and extensive appendices demonstrating technical competence
Open-source commitment to release kernels, providing value to the community
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: gather fusion, epilogue fusion, and ping-pong scheduling are known techniques; contribution is primarily engineering-driven combination and GPU specialization
Hardware-specific design tightly coupled to Hopper/Blackwell; generalizability to other accelerators unclear and limited broader impact
Fairness of baseline comparisons: ScatterMoE/MoMoE in Triton have inherent optimization limitations; DeepGEMM requires custom kernels for complete comparison
Token rounding evaluation incomplete: downstream task evaluation limited to 1.4B parameters only; improvements modest except in extreme sparsity (K/E ≤ 1/64); no full training runs on larger models
End-to-end evaluation limited: most results at layer/kernel level; full training throughput uses non-standard lm-engine codebase; no inference performance reported
Methodological concerns: memory comparison somewhat circular (SonicMoE by design materializes less); upper bounds exclude router computation; token rounding as 'drop-in replacement' overstated
Incomplete exploration of design sensitivity: limited ablation on tile sizes and warpgroup configurations; arbitrary-seeming parameter choices
Code unavailable at review time; reproducibility gaps in specific architectural choices and lm-engine integration
